clock_dir_past: बजकर is the conjunctive participle of बजना, “to hit the hour”
(en.wiktionary.org, entry “बजना”), and frames the minutes counted FORWARD
from a struck hour: “आठ बजकर बीस मिनट” is 8:20.
clock_fraction_15: सवा “and a quarter”: en.wiktionary.org, entry “सवा”, with the usage
example “सवा एक बज गए हैं” (“the time is 1:15”).  It counts FORWARD from
the hour it names, exactly as साढ़े does, hence bare_quarter_past.
clock_fraction_30: साढ़े “half past”: en.wiktionary.org, entry “साढ़े”, glossed “... and a
half” and “half past”, with the usage example “डेढ़, ढाई, और अब साढ़े तीन
बज गए हैं” (“1:30, 2:30, and now it's half past three”).  It counts
FORWARD from the hour it names, hence bare_half_past.
clock_fraction_prev_45: पौने “a quarter less”, and as a clock reading “quarter to” --
en.wiktionary.org, entry “पौने”, with the usage example “पौने दस” glossed
9:45.  It is the ASYMMETRIC member of the set: साढ़े and सवा count forward
from the hour they name, पौने counts BACK from it, so पौने दस is a quarter
short of ten and never a quarter past it.  That is why it ships in the
prev family rather than as a plain fraction.

clock_landmark_150: ढाई is the matching suppletive word for two-and-a-half --
en.wiktionary.org, entry “ढाई”: “two and a half” and “half past two”.
clock_landmark_90: डेढ़ is a fully suppletive word for one-and-a-half, and as a clock
reading it IS half past one -- en.wiktionary.org, entry “डेढ़”: “one and
a half; 1.5” and “half past one; 1:30”.  It is a literal, never composed
from a half-word plus एक, which is why it ships as a landmark at minute
90 of the day rather than as a fraction.

marker_weekday_word: को trails a weekday to mark the time at which something happens --
en.wiktionary.org, entry “को”, sense “in, at the time of”, worked example
“बुधवार को” (“on Wednesday”).  Inside a recurrence frame already opened by
हर (“हर सोमवार को” -- every Monday) the postposition is pure filler: हर has
already made the phrase recurring, and को adds nothing to the rule, so it is
swallowed into the match rather than left to strand in the remainder.
Shipped as the SINGULAR day-word only.  The plural counterpart
(marker_recur_day_word) is what LICENSES a bare postposed weekday as
recurring, and Hindi has no such form: bare “सोमवार को” names one specific
Monday, not every Monday, and is read as a single date by the grammar engine.

There is NO named_day file for any OTHER offset.  कल names BOTH
yesterday and tomorrow and परसों BOTH the day before yesterday and the
day after tomorrow -- CLDR 47 maps locale hi's relative-type--1 and
relative-type-1 to the same word कल, and its -2 and +2 to the same word
परसों, and en.wiktionary lists both senses under each entry.  Only the
verb's tense separates them, which this engine does not read, so the
words are refused rather than guessed at a direction.
